Where it goes: a cage between two vertebrae, 4–11× stiffer than the bone around it

Lumbar interbody fusion. Schematic, not to scale. Blue: shielded bone. Bone loss around stiff implants is measured clinically; fewer revisions is not proven.

Here is where the part goes: a lumbar interbody fusion cage, in the space where a disc was removed. A titanium cage is far stiffer than the bone around it, so the load funnels through the metal and the bone beside it is under-loaded and thins. A cage that matches bone shares the load, but it must still carry twice body load on its own without breaking. That tension is the goal we gave the agents, verbatim: as mechanically homogeneous with bone as possible without losing integrity.

The gap: titanium 110 GPa, cortical bone 10–30, printed resins 1–8

Ti-6Al-4V 110 GPa, cortical bone 10–30 GPa: Niinomi et al. 2016, Regen Biomater, doi:10.1093/rb/rbw016. Measured resin moduli: one specimen each, crosshead only.

On a log scale: titanium at the top, cortical bone an order of magnitude below, trabecular bone and our printed resins below that. Resins are stand-ins. The point is the gap, and that any metric for closing it can be gamed. Open-ended design judged by physics.

We measured first: Breakerspace Instron, Nov 1

Left: Tough 1500 dog-bone to fracture. Middle: AUX-1 auxetic block in compression. Right: force–displacement traces, three specimens.

Before any agent ran, we printed coupons through the PreForm API and pulled them on the Breakerspace Instron. Dog-bones to fracture, an auxetic block in compression, three traces on the screen.

Every printed part read below its datasheet; the judge used the measured values

Rigid 10K 27 % below datasheet; Tough 1500 1.5 to 22 % below. AUX-1 measured ν −0.85 to −0.95 against our frozen prediction −0.80. One specimen each.

Every resin came in below its datasheet: Rigid 10K at 8 gigapascals against 11, Tough 1500 up to 22 percent low. Those measured moduli, not the datasheet, fed the judge. The auxetic block we had predicted at minus 0.80 measured about minus 0.85 to minus 0.95.

Agents chose their instruments: PreForm as a test rig

From agent tool logs. 601 PreForm API calls across round 1. Every design had to be a real .form file.

Nobody told the agents how to use the sponsor tools. One planner agent turned the PreForm API into a measuring rig: 189 calls that write a scene, read it back and fail on any mismatch. It found that layout can rotate a part without changing its hash, and logged 38 errors along the way.

Agents chose their instruments: NVIDIA Warp on Brev GPUs

Warp numbers are single tests. Brev L40S boxes also ran the frozen judge at up to 20M unknowns. Warp was the only NVIDIA tool agents ran.

On NVIDIA, agents wrote their own Warp kernels: one timed a Warp operator about seven times faster than NumPy on one test; another checked an adjoint gradient against finite differences to 3e-4. Brev GPUs also ran our judge at sizes a laptop could not fit.

Round 1: agents go where the metric points

“This design targets the metric, not a clinical device.” — the winning agent

Official score filled every void with fused bone, so less implant looked more like bone. Winner: the 1 mm wire loop, 9 minutes in.

Round 1 scored a proxy: mismatch with every void filled by fused bone. Less implant, more bone-like. The winner was a one millimetre wire loop, done in nine minutes, whose own report says it targets the metric, not a clinical device. Singles, best-of-N, planners and collectives all read the metric within minutes and designed to it. Alan's run saw the same with a two-joint grader: one peer refused, its group gamed anyway. Organization does not control gaming. The judge has to.

Once the graft is soft, the ranking flips

Lower is better. Both lone agents failed implant-alone integrity; the loop would carry 1132 MPa against a 17 MPa limit.

Score the same designs in the early state, before the graft fuses, and the ranking flips. The designs that won by removing material fail when they have to carry load.

Inside the part: the mismatch the agents had to reason about

Strain-energy stimulus in the bone around a textbook cage and a round-1 single. Blue shielded, orange overloaded. Our judge’s solver, coarse mesh; illustrative, not a score.

This is our own solver: the strain-energy stimulus in the bone around two designs. Blue is shielded bone, orange is overloaded. This is what a good metric has to capture without being gameable.

Round 2: hold the test still, let the agents move

Worst state

Mismatch scored with voids empty and fused, keeping the worse

Implant alone

Integrity with no bone carrying load; a fail ranks below every pass

Withheld state

Early-graft value kept out of their tool

Re-scored

Frozen code, twice their resolution, by the evaluator

Six agents, no roles, 75 min: 14 designs scored, three families, three writers.

Self-policed on margin: dropped its two lowest-M designs at 15.4 and 16.0 of 17 MPa.

Shipped a 41 %-solid lattice. Predicted 14 to 15 MPa; judge measured 14.10.

Best on the state it never saw: 0.283 vs control 0.301.

Goal metric 1.75 [1.23, 2.26] vs textbook 2.28 [2.15, 2.41]: a tie, not a win.

Printed: round 2 cage (top, Tough 1500 V2, Form Studio 1) with Alan’s three mesh cages (Alpha Fast, display stand-ins)

Metric written by an agent that had seen no results, frozen before launch. One arm, one run, no control arm; it started from a lattice shape in the spec. Its own coarse 0.84 became 1.75 at full resolution.

So we held the test still and let the agents move. The new metric scores the worse of two states, voids empty and voids fused, so removing material no longer wins. Integrity is checked with the implant alone, and a fail ranks below every pass. One loading state was withheld from their tool. And everything was re-scored by the evaluator at twice the resolution. Then six agents with no roles and a shared board ran 75 minutes. They scored fourteen designs across three families. Two had lower scores than what shipped, and the group dropped both because their strength margins were thin: 15.4 and 16.0 against 17. They predicted the shipped part would come in at 14 to 15 at the judge's resolution; it came in at 14.10. On the state they never saw, it scored best of all nine designs. On the goal metric it ties the textbook cage; it does not beat it. One arm, one run, and it started from a shape the spec handed it. This is what honest looks like, not what winning looks like.

Lower is better everywhere. Frozen judge, full resolution, 20M-unknown cap. Spearman between the two rankings −0.62 (n = 8). Goal metric is post-registered and exploratory; a design that fails integrity ranks below every pass. Two replicates per arm: no arm ranking.

One table, two tests. On the round 1 metric the loop wins and the textbook cage comes last. On the goal metric the textbook cage and the round 2 collective are the only designs that pass integrity with margin, and they tie. Every other agent design fails when the implant has to carry the load alone. The withheld early state tells the same story: the round 2 cage is lowest of all nine. Lower is better everywhere.

Round 1 collective: one volunteer writer, out of credit at 15 minutes

From board posts and status logs. c1 posted “PIPELINE READY” and capped 10 s later; nobody took over; no submission.

In round 1 the leaderless group agreed on the board that one agent would write the deliverables. It posted pipeline ready and ran out of credit ten seconds later, fifteen minutes in. Nobody took over. No submission. A leaderless group still built a single point of failure.

Round 2 collective: decentralized by measurement, not by promise

Degree centralization from board logs: collectives 0.30 and 0.40, planners 1.00. Round 2: zero directive posts, three writers, three design families.

We measured decentralization rather than promising it. Board centralization 0.30 for the collectives against 1.00 for the planner teams. In round 2 that bought variety, three design families, and no single point of failure.

What it did not buy: speed, or a win over the textbook

Alan Chen, run 3: 54 runs, 9 per arm, same $12 cap. Teams cost 2 to 3× (derived from v3 means $2.98, 4.96, 8.70; cost pairs Holm p ≤ 0.0073); stiffness Holm p = 1.00 for every pair. Our n = 2: no arm ranking. Arena, guard and judge: MIT licence.

Alan's controlled version: same task, same cap, nine runs per arm. Teams spent two to three times what one agent spent, and no pair differed on stiffness. With two replicates per arm our run cannot rank arms either. So trust came from the judge, the guard and physical ground truth, not from how the agents were organized. Arena, guard and judge are open source under MIT. Credit to Alan Chen for runs 0 to 3.
